title: Is a $600 Car Payment Too Much? How to Check Against Your Pay
description: Whether a $600 car payment is too much depends on your take-home pay and your other bills. Here is the math per paycheck, with a worked example.

paa.question: Is a $600 car payment too much?
paa.answer: For many budgets, yes. A common guide keeps total car costs, including insurance and gas, under about 10% to 15% of take-home pay. A $600 payment alone fits that only if you take home roughly $4,000 to $6,000 a month and your other bills still leave room to save.

bodyHtml:
Six hundred dollars a month is a common car payment, and that is part of the problem. A payment can be normal and still be too large for your budget. The useful question is not whether $600 is a lot in general, but what share of your own paycheck it takes, and what is left for everything else once it is paid.

What $600 a Month Really Costs

Over a five-year loan, $600 a month is $36,000 in payments. At a 7% rate, that payment carries a loan of about $30,300, so roughly $5,700 of what you pay is interest.

The payment is also only part of the cost of the car. Insurance, gas, registration and maintenance come on top. For many drivers those add $250 to $400 a month, which turns a $600 payment into $850 to $1,000 of total car cost every month.

Rules of Thumb People Use

There is no single official rule, but a few guides come up again and again.

  • The payment alone at no more than about 10% of take-home pay.
  • All car costs together, including insurance, gas and upkeep, at no more than about 15% to 20% of take-home pay.
  • The 20/4/10 guide: put 20% down, finance for no more than four years, and keep total car costs under 10% of gross income.

These are deliberately conservative. They exist because a car payment is one of the few large bills you choose, and choosing a smaller one leaves room for savings, debt payoff and surprises. Our guide on how much car you can actually afford walks through the full formula.

A Worked Example, Per Paycheck

Say you take home $4,000 a month and are paid every two weeks. Each paycheck is $4,000 times 12, divided by 26, or about $1,846.

A $600 monthly payment works out to $600 times 12, divided by 26, or about $277 out of every paycheck. That is 15% of take-home pay for the payment alone. Add $300 a month for insurance and gas and total car costs reach $900, or 22.5% of take-home pay.

By the guides above, that is too much for this income. It does not mean disaster. It means less room for everything else: rent, groceries, savings and any debt you are trying to clear. The same $600 on a $6,000 take-home pay is 10%, which most guides would call comfortable.

Signs the Payment Is Squeezing Your Budget

  • Your checking balance runs close to zero before every payday.
  • Savings have stopped, or only happen in months with a third paycheck.
  • A repair or an insurance renewal goes on a credit card.
  • You owe more on the loan than the car is worth, so selling would not clear it.

If the last one is true, our guide on avoiding being upside down on a car loan covers how people get out of it.

What to Do If It Is Too Much

If you have not bought yet, shop by total price and term, not by monthly payment. A dealer can hit almost any payment by stretching the loan, which raises the total interest. A larger down payment, a shorter term and a cheaper car all lower the real cost.

If you already have the loan, three options are worth checking. Refinancing can lower the rate if your credit has improved. Paying a little extra each month shortens the loan and cuts interest. And if the car is worth more than you owe, selling and buying something cheaper can reset the whole budget.

Whatever you decide, check it against the paychecks it comes out of. Forgenta forecasts your balance to each payday with every bill on it, including the car payment, and shows what is safe to spend after it, so you can see the real squeeze before you sign.

Questions to Ask Before You Sign

A few questions catch most payments that are too large before they become a seven-year problem.

  • What is the total price, including fees and add-ons, and not just the monthly figure?
  • How many months is the loan, and what is the APR? Two offers with the same payment can differ by thousands in interest.
  • What will insurance cost on this exact car? Get a quote before you buy, not after.
  • If one paycheck came in short, which bill would you skip to make the car payment?

The last question is the honest test. If the answer is rent or groceries, the payment is too large for your budget today, whatever a dealer or a rule of thumb says.

It also helps to think about how long you will keep the car. A payment that feels fine for two years can feel very different in year five, when the car needs tires and brakes and the loan still has a year to run. Planning for the whole loan, not the first few months, is what keeps a reasonable payment reasonable.

If you are unsure, sleep on it. A good deal is rarely gone tomorrow, and a payment you can live with for five years deserves more than one afternoon at a dealership.

The Bottom Line

A $600 car payment is too much when it pushes total car costs past roughly 15% to 20% of your take-home pay or leaves nothing for savings. On a high income it can be fine. On a typical one it usually means the car is quietly crowding out everything else. Do the per-paycheck math before you sign, and keep the payment you can carry even in a month that goes wrong.

faqs.q: What is a good car payment for my income?
faqs.a: Many guides keep the payment near 10% of take-home pay and total car costs under 15% to 20%. On $4,000 a month that is about $400 for the payment.

faqs.q: Is a longer loan a good way to lower the payment?
faqs.a: It lowers the payment but raises the total interest and the chance of owing more than the car is worth. A cheaper car or a bigger down payment is usually better.

faqs.q: How much is $600 a month per paycheck?
faqs.a: About $277 if you are paid every two weeks: $600 times 12, divided by 26.
